n: Nephi quotes Isaiah 48 from the brass plates. Isaiah addresses Israel’s people, who claim God’s name but don’t worship Him sincerely. Nephi’s version adds “or out of the waters of baptism,” a phrase Joseph Smith added in the 1840 edition to clarify the meaning of “waters of Judah.”

f.g: Not in the KJV; added in the 1840 Book of Mormon edition.
KJV reads “but not in truth.” They make oaths by God without meaning them.

n: They proudly call themselves citizens of the holy city, Jerusalem, yet do not rely on God. The Book of Mormon says they “do not stay themselves” on God, where the KJV says they “stay themselves” — making clear their trust is hollow.

f.g: Hebrew YHWH Tseva’ot — the Lord of the armies of heaven.

n: God reminds Israel that He announced past events long before they happened, then suddenly brought them to pass. Fulfilled prophecy shows He is the true God.
He foretold events in advance because Israel was stubborn. A neck like iron and a forehead of brass picture rigid, unbending pride.

f.w: thy neck is an iron sinew
f.g: Stiff-necked: refusing to bow, like an ox resisting the yoke.

n: God told them ahead of time so they couldn’t credit their idols for what He had done.

f.g: An idol carved from wood or stone; a “molten image” is cast from metal.

n: They have seen and heard it all — will they not testify? Now God reveals new, hidden things. The Book of Mormon reads “seen and heard” where the KJV has “heard, see.”
These new things were not known before, so Israel cannot claim it already knew them.

f.w: lest thou shouldst say—Behold I knew them
f.g: God prevents Israel from taking credit for His revelations.

n: Israel did not listen or understand; their ears were closed. God knew they would act treacherously; from their beginnings they were rebels.
Yet for His own name’s sake God holds back His anger and does not destroy them. His mercy rests on His character, not their merit.

God has refined Israel in the “furnace of affliction,” like metal purified by fire. The Book of Mormon omits the KJV’s phrase “but not with silver.” Trials can be a means of choosing and purifying God’s people.

God acts for His own sake and will not let His name be dishonored or share His glory with idols. The Book of Mormon’s “I will not suffer my name to be polluted” replaces the KJV’s question “how should my name be polluted?”

f.w: I will not give my glory unto another

n: God calls Israel to listen: He is the first and the last, eternal and unchanging. Latter-day Saints understand the speaker, Jehovah, to be the premortal Jesus Christ, who uses the same title in Revelation.

f.w: I am the first, and I am also the last

n: God’s hand laid the earth’s foundation and stretched out the heavens; when He calls, creation stands at attention.

f.g: Measured or stretched out the sky with His hand.

n: Which idol predicted this? The Lord has chosen someone to carry out His will against Babylon and the Chaldeans — historically Cyrus of Persia, who conquered Babylon in 539 BC. The Book of Mormon adds that God will fulfill the word declared by His prophets.

f.g: The ruling people of the Neo-Babylonian empire.

f.w: he will do his pleasure on Babylon

n: The Lord has called this deliverer and will make his mission succeed.
God has spoken openly from the beginning, not in secret. The speaker says the Lord God and His Spirit have sent him — words many see as pointing to a prophet or to the Messiah.

f.w: I have not spoken in secret

n: The Redeemer, the Holy One of Israel, teaches His people what is truly good and leads them in the right way.

f.w: thy Redeemer, the Holy One of Israel

f.g: Teaches you what is truly for your benefit.

n: A tender lament: if only Israel had obeyed, their peace would have flowed like a river and their righteousness rolled in like ocean waves — steady and endless.

f.w: thy peace been as a river

n: Their descendants would have been as countless as sand, and their name would never have been cut off — the Abrahamic promise fulfilled.

f.g: Your own children; “bowels” was a KJV way of saying “body” or “inner parts.”

n: A joyful command: leave Babylon, flee the Chaldeans, and proclaim to the whole earth that the Lord has redeemed Israel. In the latter days “Babylon” also symbolizes worldliness that God’s people must flee.
Just as God gave water from the rock in the Exodus, He will care for those returning home through the desert.

f.w: waters to flow out of the rock

n: Despite all God has done — the Book of Mormon adds “and greater also” — the wicked will find no peace.

f.w: there is no peace, saith the Lord, unto the wicked
